structure.overview: The case concerns the Applicant's judicial review of the Minister's decision to deny waiver of tax penalties for RRSP over-contributions in 2018. The Applicant argued a misunderstanding of spousal RRSP rules caused the over-contribution, while the Minister found no reasonable error was established. The Federal Court dismissed the judicial review, finding the Minister's decision reasonable and justified.

party_points.text: misunderstood spousal RRSP rules causing over-contribution
asserted honest error, prompt correction, negative interest impact
new ground about lack of CRA definition of 'reasonable error'
request to waive cost order from prior motion

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant over-contributed to RRSPs in 2018 and was assessed tax by the Minister, who denied his waiver request; he seeks judicial review.

citations.cite: section 204.1 of Part X.1 of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)
citations.why: Legal basis for tax on RRSP over-contribution

citations.cite: section 204.1(4)
citations.why: Minister's discretion to waive tax

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the Minister's decision reasonable and dismisses the judicial review application.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant's RRSPs included a personal and a spousal RRSP since 2010.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In 2018, the Applicant contributed more than his allowable RRSP limit.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In March 2019, the Applicant requested waiver of penalties, explaining he misunderstood spousal RRSP contribution rules and would withdraw excess.
idea_list: Explanation of misunderstanding about spousal RRSPs

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In March 2019, the Applicant filed a T1-OVP return and paid $1,008.25 tax for 2018 over-contribution.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In May 2019, the Minister assessed $1,040.53 tax with no penalty; arrears interest was adjusted to nil and balance paid by Applicant.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: On September 30, 2019, the Minister denied the waiver, explaining reasonable error excludes misunderstanding RRSP limits and the Applicant's circumstances were not reasonable.

citations.cite: Subsection 204.1(4) of the Income Tax Act
citations.why: Minister's discretion to waive tax explained

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: On October 9, 2019, the Applicant requested a second review, asserting honest error, prompt correction, and negative interest impact.
idea_list: Explanation of error and correction steps

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: On March 4, 2020, the Minister denied the second request, emphasizing Applicant's long awareness of limits and no reasonable error established.

citations.cite: Perinpanayagam v TFSA Processing Unit, 2020 FC 1111 at para 41
citations.why: Minister not obliged to advise on reasonable error

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Respondent raised preliminary issues from the Applicant's affidavit and memorandum, which the Court discussed with parties.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The first preliminary issue is whether to strike paragraph 6 and exhibit C of the Applicant's affidavit as not before the decision-maker.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court strikes paragraph 6 and exhibit C as not before the decision-maker and finds them irrelevant to the Minister's decision on reasonable steps.
idea_list: Evidence irrelevant as Minister made no decision on reasonable steps

citations.cite: Tsleil-Waututh Nation v Canada (Attorney General), 2017 FCA 128 at para 86
citations.why: Only evidence before decision-maker admissible on judicial review

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The second issue is whether the Applicant can raise a new ground about lack of CRA definition of 'reasonable error' not pleaded in Notice of Application.
idea_list: Respondent objects citing Tl’azt’en Nation v Sam
Applicant argues it's related to reasonableness

citations.cite: Tl’azt’en Nation v Sam, 2013 FCA 226
citations.why: Respondent relies on it to oppose new ground of review

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court refuses to exercise discretion to allow the new ground, finding it tangential and without merit as Minister provided guidance and no duty to advise.
idea_list: Discretion not exercised to allow new ground
Minister provided guidance on reasonable error

citations.cite: Perinpanayagam v TFSA Processing Unit, 2020 FC 1111 at para 41
citations.why: Minister not obliged to advise on reasonable error

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The third issue is the Applicant's request to waive a cost order from a prior unsuccessful motion, arguing it was unnecessary if Minister had waived taxes.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court dismisses the cost waiver request as moot due to dismissal and notes proper appeal procedure was not followed.
idea_list: Application dismissed so cost waiver moot
Proper appeal procedure for cost order not followed

citations.cite: Rule 51 of the Federal Courts Rules
citations.why: Proper procedure to appeal cost order

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The sole remaining issue is whether the Minister's refusal to waive the Part X.1 tax was unreasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court agrees with the Respondent that the standard of review is reasonableness, citing Vavilov and Canada Post Corp.
idea_list: Cites Vavilov and Canada Post Corp

citations.cite: Canada (MCI) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at paras 23, 25
citations.why: Sets reasonableness as presumptive standard of review

citations.cite: Canada Post Corp v Canadian Union of Postal Workers, 2019 SCC 67
citations.why: Explains what is required for reasonable decision

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section 204.1(4) of the ITA allows the Minister to waive Part X.1 tax if the excess arose from reasonable error and reasonable steps are taken to eliminate it.
idea_list: Conditions: reasonable error and reasonable steps

citations.cite: Section 204.1(4) of the ITA
citations.why: Statutory text of waiver provision

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: A taxpayer must satisfy the Minister that the excess arose from reasonable error and that reasonable steps are being taken to eliminate it.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal in Connolly held subsection 204.1(4) aims to relieve harsh tax for reasonable mistakes corrected by reasonable steps.

citations.cite: Connolly v Canada (Minister of National Revenue), 2019 FCA 161 at para 66
citations.why: Explains purpose of subsection 204.1(4)

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Connolly held reasonableness requires objective assessment; ignorance of limits is not reasonable, but misinformation after inquiry might be.
idea_list: Misinformation after inquiry may be reasonable
Reliance on third party not determinative

citations.cite: Connolly v Canada (Minister of National Revenue), 2019 FCA 161 at para 69
citations.why: Sets test for reasonable error under subsection 204.1(4)

citations.cite: R. v. McKinlay Transport Ltd., 1990 CanLII 137 (SCC), [1990] 1 S.C.R. 627 at p. 636, 106 N.R. 385
citations.why: Supports self-assessment obligation

citations.cite: Guindon v. Canada, 2015 SCC 41, [2015] 3 S.C.R. 3 at para. 54
citations.why: Supports self-assessment obligation

citations.cite: Dimovski v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2011 FC 721 at paras 16-17
citations.why: Supports self-assessment obligation

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: In Connolly, the Court found the Minister's decision reasonable as the applicant gave little explanation or inquiry about his mistake.

citations.cite: Connolly v Canada (Minister of National Revenue), 2019 FCA 161
citations.why: Example of reasonable decision on similar facts

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant claims he misunderstood spousal RRSP rules, believing contributions counted against spouse's limit, causing over-contribution.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court rejects innocence as test; reasonableness of error matters, and taxpayers must ensure compliance or seek advice.

citations.cite: Lepiarczyk v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2008 FC 1022 at para 19
citations.why: Reasonableness of error is test

citations.cite: Connolly, supra at para 69
citations.why: Self-assessment obligation

citations.cite: Dimovski v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2011 FC 721 at paras 16-17
citations.why: Self-assessment obligation

citations.cite: Perinpanayagam, supra at para 38
citations.why: Self-assessment obligation

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant did not provide evidence of how he made the mistake or sought advice, similar to Connolly's insufficient evidence.

citations.cite: Connolly, supra
citations.why: Applicant's evidence similar to Connolly's insufficient evidence

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Minister reasonably concluded the Applicant did not establish reasonable error, providing a rational chain of analysis.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Minister's decision is justified, transparent, intelligible, and within acceptable outcomes; judicial review is dismissed.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Respondent is entitled to costs of $1,000; the amount is reasonable under Tariff B.

citations.cite: Tariff B
citations.why: Guideline for costs quantum

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains that a reasonable decision must be coherent, rational, and justified by facts and law, citing Vavilov and related cases.

citations.cite: Vavilov, at para. 85
citations.why: Defines reasonable decision as coherent and justified

citations.cite: Vavilov, at para. 84
citations.why: Reviewing court must examine reasons with respectful attention

citations.cite: Dunsmuir, at para. 48
citations.why: Supports respectful attention to decision maker's reasoning

citations.cite: Vavilov, at para. 97
citations.why: Reasons read holistically and contextually

citations.cite: Newfoundland Nurses
citations.why: Supports holistic reading of reasons

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states that reasonableness depends on legal and factual context and must show justification, transparency, and intelligibility, citing Vavilov and other cases.

citations.cite: Vavilov, at para. 90
citations.why: Reasonableness depends on legal and factual context

citations.cite: Vavilov, at para. 99
citations.why: Decision must show justification, transparency, intelligibility

citations.cite: Dunsmuir, at paras. 47 and 74
citations.why: Supports hallmarks of reasonableness

citations.cite: Catalyst Paper Corp. v. North Cowichan (District), 2012 SCC 2, [2012] 1 S.C.R. 5, at para. 13
citations.why: Supports hallmarks of reasonableness

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains that the party challenging a decision bears the burden to prove it unreasonable by showing significant flaws, citing Vavilov.

citations.cite: Vavilov, at para. 100
citations.why: Sets burden on challenger to prove unreasonableness
